source.title: Examining Language Model Performance with Reconstructed Activations using Sparse Autoencoders

record.tranche_reason: Evaluates SAE reconstruction and its effect on GPT-2-small using activation and benchmark measurements, rather than testing the toy-model geometry in the claim.
record.gate_note: The post reports SAE reconstruction metrics and downstream effects of replacing residual-stream activations with SAE reconstructions. Its results test the SAE-recovery part of V4, not whether features are distributed across neurons. It does not provide ground-truth features to verify recovery directly. Results cited from other work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The post stress-tests released GPT-2-small residual-stream SAEs. It reports reconstruction fidelity (ℓ0, MSE, ℓ1) and the downstream loss and benchmark accuracy when activations are replaced by SAE reconstructions. On-distribution results bear weakly on V4: sparse dictionaries reconstruct activations reasonably at ≤128 tokens. Most results bear on V5. Reconstructions are incomplete, degrade the model's performance, fail to compose across layers, and break down beyond the SAE training context. That shows SAE features are not a complete or robust account of the representation.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Add that for short contexts SAE performance worsens with layer, presumably from more features than SAE width allows, while for long contexts early layers (~2–4) are worst. Also add that CE on random tokens does not map one-to-one to benchmark performance.
record.recipe_differences: Uses released GPT-2-small residual-stream SAEs and evaluates reconstruction and downstream behavior; it does not reproduce toy-model superposition experiments or measure feature-vector geometry.
record.method_sensitivity: Context position relative to SAE training context length; model layer; task/dataset (random Open WebText next-token prediction, Lambada, and CBT).

fits_no_version.finding: Feature-level histograms: most SAE features are active mainly when the intervention lowers correct-answer log-probability, and a small family is mostly 'helpful'.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Individual SAE features differ in whether their reconstruction preserves task-relevant information.

fits_no_version.finding: CE loss on random tokens does not track benchmark accuracy under SAE replacement. For example, layer 11 has similar CE to layer 10 but worse Lambada accuracy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE evaluation by CE recovered is an incomplete proxy for downstream fidelity.

record.problems: Evidence is from one model and one released SAE set. Many reported results are plots without numerical values in the text, and the study has no ground-truth feature set for verifying what the SAEs recover. The authors note that CE on random tokens does not map one-to-one to benchmark performance; the post also notes and fixes a bug in a figure.
record.rows_left_out: No separately reported numerical values were available in the text for individual layers in the Open WebText, Lambada, or CBT plots; the grouped figure-only outcomes are recorded instead. Other plotted metrics and feature-level histograms are not included because they do not directly measure whether SAE features recover the representations named by V4.

untested.parts: All of it: toy-model geometry, sparsity transition, near-orthogonality.
All of it: capacity competition and dedicated dimensions for important features.
Whether features are spread across many neurons. Recovery against ground-truth features, and interpretability of the recovered features.
Stability across seeds or dictionary sizes, and canonicality (whether different SAEs find the same features).

missing.what: Within the training context, SAE performance (reconstruction and ΔCE) worsens with layer. The authors attribute this to later layers having more features than a fixed-width SAE can resolve.
CBT middle layers (2–5) show very high variance in Δlnp and can 'totally ruin' the correct answer.

record.verdict_notes: The reader linked everything to V4. But the long-context, downstream and composition rows show SAE reconstructions are incomplete or non-robust, which bears on V5 rather than on whether sparse features exist. Evidence is from one model and one released SAE set, with values mostly figure-only. LessWrong comments (e.g. loss low up to ~200 tokens) are not the study's results.

versions.untested_parts: Toy-model feature overlap, near-orthogonality, sparsity-dependent transitions, and regular geometry.
Whether capacity competition causes polysemanticity or important features receive dedicated dimensions.
Whether polysemanticity can arise for reasons other than capacity pressure.
The study tests SAE reconstruction and downstream effects in GPT-2-small, but not whether real-model features spread across neurons, nor recovery against known ground-truth features.
Feature completeness, stability, and canonical status are not tested.
Feature dimensionality and whether represented features are 1-D directions are not tested.

relation.reason: It measures reconstruction fidelity and model behavior under SAE replacement, directly testing dictionary completeness in the stated conditions.

tranche.reason: The study directly identifies incomplete reconstruction and downstream behavioral failures of existing SAE dictionaries, qualifying V5.

source_check.notes: V5 evidence concerns completeness of these released SAEs; canonicality and seed stability are untested. Author comments clarify that later layers can remain effective to approximately 200 tokens, so 128 is the training length rather than a universal abrupt failure boundary.
